items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: Kid Renee, oh, that's a little good sort of plays then. Kid Renee, he was there too.

ctx.x: Just when he was making it again, he died. Did you ever have any battles of music like with Charlie Cook or anybody like that? No, in Chicago, you never had. You see,

you know, I remember those days. Kid Renee, oh, that's a little good sort of plays then. Kid Renee, he was there too. Chalky Banana. Dead. Oh, these wagons, you know. You know, in the corner there, I saw these balls like on a Sunday night, Sunday afternoon, going different neighborhoods and they battle. These were hellfire days in the morning. That was the second line, following the band all over the street. Did you play parade yourself? Yes. I played one or two before I went to the hood. But who? Manny Parism,…
Yeah. OBB, huh? Did you play the E flat then? Yes. I learned on the E flat when I was a kid. My fingers
And when you started having lessons, you started to read straight away?

Did you? Well, I had to. No, no. Yeah. Papa, he gave me lessons a few months before he let me play the horn. He wanted me to get the rudiments of the music. Because he said, you've got plenty of time to learn this jazz. He used to call it ragtime then. There was no such thing as jazz when I was learning. He said, you've got plenty of time for that. Learn those notes. And he says, one note played right is better than two, three dozen notes all jumbled up and what not. He said, that's not music. I want you to learn…
Kid Reno was the first one. That's another one. He was a creator. Kid Reno was the first one making high notes.
